## Shakshuka — Meaning, Origin & Etymology | The Journey
Jewish immigrants from North Africa — primarily Tunisia, Libya, and Morocco — brought shakshuka to Israel in the 1950s. The dish became associated with Israeli breakfast culture so thoroughly that many Israelis assumed it was Israeli. Haaretz columnist Ronit Vered documented its Libyan-Tunisian origins in the 2000s, to considerable surprise. [...] ### Today Shakshuka demonstrates how food travels faster than acknowledgment. Israeli cafés served it for decades before the world knew it existed. North African Jewish immigrants brought it; Israel made it famous; the internet spread it globally. The origin story arrived long after the recipe. [...] The dish's origin is contested in the way all beloved foods' origins are contested. Tunisia claims it as Tunisian. Libya claims it. plan.title: Shakshuka: How Eggs in Tomato Sauce Conquered Brunch
plan.description: Shakshuka is a North African dish of eggs poached in spiced tomato and pepper sauce. Follow its journey from the Maghreb to Israeli kitchens and brunch tables around the world.

beats.narration: Eggs poached in a bubbling red sauce, served right in the pan. Millions of people think they know where it comes from. Many of them are surprised by the real answer.
This is shakshuka. Eggs gently cooked in a sauce of tomatoes, olive oil, peppers, onion and garlic, usually spiced with cumin, paprika and cayenne.
The name is a clue. In Tunisian Arabic, shakshuka means mixed. In Algerian Arabic it means a mixture. It may also echo the sound of sizzling and bubbling.

props.definition: Means "mixture" or "mixed" in North African Arabic dialects, and may echo the sound of bubbling.

beats.narration: Most histories point to the Maghreb, especially Tunisia and Libya. Cooks there already made vegetable stews in olive oil. Eggs and tomato joined them later.
Why later? Tomatoes and peppers come from the Americas. They only reached North Africa after the sixteenth century. So the dish as we know it could not exist before that.

props.image_query: fresh red tomatoes and peppers market

beats.narration: There is a lookalike word. Turkish şakşuka is an oily vegetable dish, but it has no eggs. The similar name may simply be a coincidence.
Tunisian cooks vary it with the season. Artichokes, broad beans or carrots can replace tomatoes. Libyan versions are said to be especially spicy, sometimes with dried lamb jerky.

First, tomatoes and peppers reach North Africa. Then, in the 1950s, immigrants bring it to Israel. Finally, in the 2000s, its origins are documented, to surprise, since many Israelis thought it was Israeli.

events.label: Tomatoes and peppers reach North Africa

beats.narration: From Israeli cafés, the internet carried it everywhere. Today it fills brunch menus around the world. Food, it turns out, often travels faster than credit.
So next time you dip bread into that red sauce, remember. It is a North African classic, made famous by migration, and still bubbling after centuries.

props.text: A North African classic, carried across the world by the people who cooked it.
